1.pericope_label: Be ye holy: parents, sabbaths, idols and the peace offering

schools.summary: Calvin takes the opening command as the key to all that follows, since men are not to measure the service of God by their own conceits but by his nature, and must begin by purifying themselves, being recalled to the imitation of God who in adopting them meant that they should bear his image; Gill notes that the offering in view must be the vow or freewill kind.

Henry infers from the address to the whole congregation that all were concerned to know their duty, and remarks that even in the darker ages of the law, that religion could not be of God which boasted of ignorance as its mother; he reads the pairing of the sabbath with the fifth commandment as a charge to parents, and observes that the ruin of young people has often begun in contempt of parents and profanation of the day.

Clarke translates elilim literally as nothings, the very word the apostle used in saying that an idol is nothing in the world; Wesley reads the sabbath clause as a limit set on filial obedience, since children must not obey a parent who commands the profanation of the day.

Ellicott calls the chapter an embodying of the Decalogue, counts sixteen groups of precepts bound together by the refrain I am the Lord, marks the address to all the congregation as a phrase found only once more in the Pentateuch, notes that the mother is named before the father in only three places of Scripture, and explains the transition to the peace offering from Israel's habit of sacrificing to idols the beasts meant for their own table; Keil and Delitzsch call the command to be holy both the principle of all that follows and the goal Israel was to keep in view.

debates.question: Why is the sabbath joined to the commandment about parents?

sides.position: to limit filial obedience — if parents command the profanation of the day, the children must not obey
to charge parents to use their authority for the honour of God’s sabbaths

themes: ye shall be holy, for I am holy
fear thy mother and thy father
idols that are nothings
the flesh not eaten on the third day

9.pericope_label: Gleanings, honest dealing, and the deaf and the blind

schools.summary: Calvin reads the group as one prohibition worked out in its parts, since God enumerates as thefts the cases where either deceit or violence is used, and presses hardest on the hireling, who lives from hand to mouth, so that a rich man who keeps him in suspense deprives him as it were of life; he sets the deaf and the blind under the sixth commandment, since to insult the deaf is no less absurd than to assail stones with reproaches. Gill adds Aben Ezra's word that he who sees a theft and keeps silent is himself as the thief, and the rabbinic chain by which stealing leads to dealing falsely, and lying to the oath.

Henry holds that whatever we have in the world we must see to be honestly come by, since we cannot be truly rich, nor long rich, with what is not; he calls the deferring of a labourer's wages a sin that cries to heaven for vengeance, and reports that the Jewish writers thought no one could be barbarous enough for the literal stumbling-block.
Clarke says that a man capable of putting a stumbling-block before the blind must have a heart cased with cruelty; Wesley traces the same descent from lying to perjury.

Ellicott makes the gleaning laws part of the chapter's holiness, notes that fixing the poor man's right in law releases him from a private charity that might have been capricious and tyrannical, reports the sixtieth part left at the field's far end and the three hours at which the poor came, ties the command against stealing back to the owners of fields who withhold it, and explains the closing clause: God hears when the human ear is stopped, and sees when the human eye is extinct; Keil and Delitzsch add the olive-yard, where shaking the boughs for what the sticks had missed was expressly forbidden.

debates.question: Is the stumbling-block before the blind literal or figurative?

sides.position: literal — a man capable of it has a heart cased with cruelty
figurative, as the interpretation of Christ’s time had it: imposing on the ignorant and misdirecting those who ask advice

themes: the corner of the field and the gleanings
the wages of the hireling
thou shalt not curse the deaf
a stumblingblock before the blind

15.pericope_label: Judgment without partiality, and the talebearer

schools.summary: Calvin reports two derivations of the word for the talebearer, one from the merchant, since the whisperer is no less busy hunting false reports than the trader is bent on buying and selling, and one from the foot, calumniators being always on the move; his own account is of vagabonds who penetrate everybody's secrets to bring quiet people into trouble. Gill divides the charge in judgment between the judge who pronounces and the witness who testifies, and reaches the duty of rescue from the verse that follows.

Clarke will not restrain himself about the slanderer, who gets the secrets of every person and family and retails them wherever he goes, than which a more despicable character does not exist; Wesley reads the second clause of the false witness, noting that accusers and witnesses stand while the judges sit.

Ellicott reads the judgment law as a correction of the verse before it, so that consideration for the infirm must not follow the poor man into court, quotes the second-Temple case of the rich man who would let the poor win to spare him the humiliation of alms, and takes standing against a neighbour's blood literally, as a duty of rescue at the hazard of one's own life; Keil and Delitzsch put the two halves in two verbs, to act partially out of unmanly pity and to adorn the person of the great.

debates.question: What does it mean to stand against the blood of thy neighbour?

sides.position: a duty of rescue — not to stand by while a man drowns or is set upon, and not to keep silent in court when one knows the truth
a prohibition of false witness, by which an innocent man’s life is endangered

themes: respect not the person of the poor
nor honour the person of the mighty
thou shalt not go about as a talebearer
stand not against the blood of thy neighbour

17.pericope_label: Hatred, rebuke, and love thy neighbour

schools.summary: Calvin makes the verse the proof that the sixth commandment reaches inward, murder being forbidden not only by hand or weapon but in the cherishing of hatred, which confirms Paul's word that the law is spiritual and refutes those who pretend Moses was an earthly lawgiver like Lycurgus or Solon; on the rebuke he warns against the rigid censors who publish their brother's defects, since whoever triumphs in his infamy precipitates his ruin, and he turns the closing precept against the schools, which taught that a man must love himself first and his neighbour by that rule. Gill gives the two ways hatred shows itself, in not saving a neighbour's life and in not reproving him.

Clarke gives the practical form of the private rebuke, to speak to the man alone or else write so that he alone shall see it, and removes the common mistake that loving one's neighbour as oneself was first instituted under the gospel; Wesley holds that a man who neither divulges his brother's wrong nor tells him of it, but smothers his hatred in sullen silence, is hating him in the act of keeping quiet, and reads as thyself of sincerity rather than equality of affection.

Ellicott illustrates vengeance and the grudge by degree from the rabbis, the refused sickle answered by the refused hatchet, and the grudge broken even by lending with a word of reproach attached; he recalls Hillel giving the whole Law negatively and notes that Christ gives it positively; Keil and Delitzsch settle the disputed phrase to mean bringing sin upon oneself rather than bearing it on the offender's account.

debates.question: Is self-love the rule by which love of neighbour is measured?

sides.position: no — God did not set self-love up as the standard; it blinds us and is the parent of all iniquities, and the command cures it by transferring the love elsewhere
the phrase measures sincerity of affection, not its equality

themes: thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart
thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour
thou shalt not avenge nor bear a grudge
thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself

19.pericope_label: Mingled kinds, and the betrothed bondmaid

schools.summary: Gill marks the change of kind, from laws planted in the heart and agreeable to the light of nature to laws of positive institution, which Jarchi calls the decree of a king who gives no reason for it; Calvin will not let the mitigated penalty be misread, since before God there is no difference between bond and free and the crime deserves death, the sentence being softened only in consideration of the people's infirmity, and the expiation still required of a man already scourged shows that an offence is not to be measured by its punishment.

Henry states the rule of the mixtures in two halves, that as what God has joined we must not separate, so what he has separated we must not join, and finds the law's own balance in the bondmaid's case: it was for the honour of marriage, though only begun by betrothing, that the crime should be punished at all, and for the honour of freedom that it should not be punished as the debauching of a free woman.

Clarke prefers plain husbandry where he can get it, since oats and wheat sown together leave the one injured and the other ruined, confesses that nobody knows what the word for the mixed garment means, and supposes a slave to have less self-command and so less guilt; Wesley gathers three purposes at once, to restrain men who would amend the works of God, to teach abhorrence of unnatural lusts by a restraint laid on the brutes, and to warn Israel off mixture with the nations.

Ellicott traces how far the prohibitions were held to reach, the produce of mixtures never being forbidden so that mules were freely used, the seed law binding only in the Holy Land and only for food crops, the rule extended to grafting, and a woollen coat not to be mended with flaxen thread; he explains that the bondmaid's espousal was not legally complete, so that she was not properly another man's wife; Keil and Delitzsch see the personal rights of a slave upheld here, so that a maid was not degraded into mere property.

debates.question: What is the reason behind the laws of mingled kinds?

sides.position: a divine distinction in creation, which man dissolves by uniting dissimilar things
largely prudential — bad husbandry, and in the garment a curb on finery
a barrier against mixture with the nations in marriage and in religion

themes: thou shalt not sow thy field with mingled seed
a garment of linen and woollen
the bondmaid betrothed and not free
the ram of the trespass offering

23.pericope_label: The uncircumcised fruit of the young trees

schools.summary: Calvin reads the law under the first commandment, the circumcision of trees letting the Jews see a symbol of their own adoption in the orchard and teaching that whatever the earth produces is in a manner profane until purified, all things being sanctified by the word of God and prayer — not that anything is impure in itself, but that the earth has contracted pollution from the corruption of man; Gill notes with Jarchi that the fourth year's fruit might be redeemed instead of given, as the tithe was.

Clarke sees no reason to look for mystical meanings, the fruit of a young tree being poor because its juices are not yet elaborated; Wesley takes the rule to serve both the trees, which grow faster for being stripped early, and the men, who are taught to bridle their appetites, and adds that part of the fourth year's produce went to the widow, the fatherless and the stranger.

Ellicott agrees that the Lawgiver enacts what careful husbandmen had always done, since early fruit is stunted and pinching it off makes the tree bear better, counts this among the four laws in Leviticus given prospectively, and reports how narrowly its scope was drawn — Canaanite plantings exempt, and no advantage of any kind to be taken of the first three years, the fruit burnt or buried rather than sold; Keil and Delitzsch keep to the grammar, where the verb formed from the noun means to treat a thing as uncircumcised, that is, to throw it away as uneatable.

debates.question: Why must the first three years’ fruit be thrown away?

sides.position: plain husbandry — the fruit is poor and the tree bears better for being stripped; there is no need to seek mystical meanings
a symbol under the first commandment, that the earth’s produce is profane until purified and that only God’s children may feed on it

themes: three years shall it be as uncircumcised
the fourth year holy to the Lord
in the fifth year ye shall eat
that it may yield unto you the increase

26.pericope_label: Eating with the blood, enchantments, hair and beard

schools.summary: Gill has from Maimonides the Zabian practice behind the clause, the blood of sacrifices gathered into a vessel or a hole in the earth with the worshippers sitting round to eat beside it, reckoning that they thereby fraternised with the demons whose food they took blood to be; Calvin states the reason behind the whole group, that God meant to sever his people from the heathen by setting an obstacle in the way, since there is nothing to which men are more prone than conforming to the customs of others.

Clarke keeps the derivation of observing times from the clouds, adds the Macians of Libya who left a tuft on the crown, and shows what the dedicated hair was for, since Achilles cut off at the pyre of Patroclus the locks his father had vowed to the river Sperchius; Wesley turns the prohibition forward, since it was unpardonable in men entrusted with the oracles of God to ask counsel of the devil, and worse in Christians who have their nativities cast or their fortunes told.

Ellicott reports the five distinct prohibitions the second Temple found in the words, all resting on the literal rendering ye shall not eat by the blood, illustrates enchantment with a list of omens a man was forbidden to read, and explains the beard by what it was worth, the greatest ornament of a man and as dear to him as life; Keil and Delitzsch read the first clause as flesh not entirely cleansed of blood, and derive the words for the forbidden arts from whispering or from the serpent, and from the eye rather than the cloud.

debates.question: What does eating with the blood forbid?

sides.position: flesh not entirely cleansed of blood — a strengthening of the earlier law, not a repetition
five distinct cases, from flesh still trembling to the meal eaten on the day of an execution
the Zabian rite of eating beside the gathered blood to fraternise with demons

themes: ye shall not eat with the blood
neither shall ye use enchantment
nor observe times
the rounded head and the marred beard

schools.summary: Gill gathers the mourning customs in detail, from the Scythians who for a dead king cut the ear and the arms and drove arrows through the left hand, to the Roman women whose tearing of their cheeks had to be forbidden by the law of the twelve tables, all of it done, on Varro's authority, to appease the infernal deities.

Clarke reaches for Virgil, where the sister of Dido fouls her face with her nails and beats her breast with her fists, and finds the same practice wherever men carry a mark in honour of what they worship, from the sectarian marks of the Hindoo castes to the crosses he has seen pricked into men's arms and rubbed with a blue colouring never afterwards effaced, hearing it behind the mark of the beast and behind Paul's word that he bore in his body the marks of the Lord Jesus; Wesley notes only that the Gentiles did this both in idol worship and in their solemn mournings.

Ellicott states why the Israelite may not, being created in the image of God and bound not to sorrow as others which have no hope, describes the printed marks as punctures filled with ink or stibium worn by slave, soldier and worshipper alike, and finds the law's own substitute in the phylactery; Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as two prohibitions of one thing, and note that the practice apparently held its ground among the Israelites in spite of it.

themes: cuttings in the flesh for the dead
nor print any marks upon you
the body that bears God’s image
the phylactery instead of the mark

29.pericope_label: Prostitution, the sanctuary, and familiar spirits

schools.summary: Gill points to the Canaanite practice of women prostituting themselves in the shrines of the idols, and explains the word for those with familiar spirits as meaning bottles, whether from what the diviner sat on, or divined by, or the swelling out of his body when he answered; Calvin widens the first law rather than narrowing it, holding that to read it of spiritual fornication is tame and forced and that those who confine it to public brothels restrict it too much, and ties the sabbath to the sanctuary by an indissoluble bond, since it would be mere mockery to rest without an ulterior object.

Henry brings the sanctuary law forward, since no place is now holy by institution as the tabernacle was, but the law still binds us to respect the assemblies of Christians, held under a promise of Christ's presence; and he notes that resorting to familiar spirits was the sin which completed the wickedness of Saul.

Clarke supplies the commercial form of temple prostitution from Justin, the Cyprian women earning by it the portion their husbands received with them at marriage, matches the diviner's inflation with Virgil's Sibyl, and presses the law past its letter against every pretender to the knowledge of the future, since God in great mercy hid it from man and gave him hope in its place; Wesley takes wizards for those who have entered into covenant with the devil.

Ellicott names the worship of Astarte, gives the practical shape reverence for the sanctuary took — no staff in the hand, no shoes on the feet, no working clothes, no money bags, no spitting and no thoroughfare, the last being what lay behind Christ's refusal to let a vessel be carried through the Temple — and describes what the wizards did with the bone of the bird yaduâ; Keil and Delitzsch insist the whoredom meant is fleshly and not spiritual, and take the other word for a departed spirit called up to disclose the future.

debates.question: How far does the law against prostituting a daughter reach?

sides.position: to all connection out of wedlock; confining it to public brothels restricts it too much, and reading it of spiritual fornication is tame and forced
to the consecrated prostitution of the idol temples, which is the practice in view

themes: do not prostitute thy daughter
keep my sabbaths and reverence my sanctuary
them that have familiar spirits
neither seek after wizards

32.pericope_label: The hoary head and the stranger

schools.summary: Calvin makes the honour due to age a matter of nature and not of statute only, since some sparks of God's majesty shine out in old men, and proves it from the old man at Athens who found no room among his countrymen until the Spartan ambassador received him, at which the Lacedaemonian cried that the Athenians knew what was right and would not do it; on the stranger he explains why the case had to be named at all, since Israel would otherwise have thought that injuring no one of their own nation discharged the whole duty. Gill fixes sixty for old age and seventy for grey hairs, and would extend the stranger to a proselyte of the gate or to any man providentially cast among them.

Clarke calls the law for the stranger humane and politic at once, since none is so desolate as a stranger and the man unmoved by that desolation has neither benevolence nor charity, while as policy it drew people to settle rather than merely sojourn; Wesley grounds the rising up on the fear of God, the respect being due for God's sake if not for the man's, old age being his singular blessing.

Ellicott grounds reverence for age in the divine title itself, since he who requires it is called the Ancient of days, and passes on the sayings that a man who cares for an old man is rewarded as though he had received God, and that prophets are believed only when armed with miracles but old men always; on the stranger he notes that not vexing him forbids the words foreigner and neophyte, and that this one law drew so many into the land that Solomon could count a hundred and fifty thousand; Keil and Delitzsch say God is honoured in the old man, and that the law goes past forbearance to love.

outliers.note: Concedes that many old men subvert their own dignity by levity or lewdness or sloth, and that grey hairs are not always accompanied by wisdom, yet holds age venerable in itself because God has commanded it.

themes: rise up before the hoary head
and fear thy God
vex not the stranger
ye were strangers in the land of Egypt

35.pericope_label: Just weights and measures, and the conclusion

schools.summary: Calvin allows that judgment may be taken strictly of judges but passes on, since the word often means rectitude, and treats false measure as a social rather than a commercial crime, for if the laws of buying and selling are corrupted human society is in a manner dissolved and the man who cheats with a false weight differs little from him who utters false coin; he reads the closing formula as the preface to the law repeated, God arguing partly from his authority as Creator and partly from the blessing of redemption. Gill adds from Jarchi why the two subjects belong together, a measurer being himself a judge.

Clarke divides the field into four heads which between them take in everything that can pass between a man and his fellow — judgment, the mete-yard, weight and measure — and lists the vessels of capacity down to the kab and the log; Wesley puts the conclusion in a sentence, that God's deliverances are not indulgences to sin but greater obligations to every duty towards God and men.

Ellicott notices that the words used of the balance are those used earlier of the bench, so that a man who calls a false measure legal is as much a corrupt judge as one who knowingly passes a wrong sentence, reports the five charges the second Temple laid against him and the rule that weights be made of polished rock rather than metal that rusts, and sizes the ephah and the hin; Keil and Delitzsch add what Deuteronomy forbids in renewing the law, stone and stone in the bag, a full measure to buy with and a scant one to sell by.

debates.question: How is the promise attached to just weights to be understood?

sides.position: the connection of long life with a just weight is figurative; God holds out to the avaricious the very thing they overvalue, to draw them from covetousness
the sin is graver than incest and equal to denying the redemption from Egypt, and was met with public inspectors and the severest penalties

themes: no unrighteousness in meteyard, weight or measure
just balances and just weights
the ephah and the hin
observe all my statutes and do them
